title: Iron-On Transfer Flip
story: A print shop is making family-reunion T-shirts. The design is a family tree of boxes, each holding a person's id, with at most two children under each box. Iron-on transfer paper prints mirror-image, so the design must be flipped left to right first. Flipping does more than swap the two halves at the top: every branch, all the way down, ends up the other way round.
task: Write mirrorDesign(root). Turn the tree into its mirror image: at every node, the left subtree becomes the right subtree and the right becomes the left. Return the root of the mirrored tree. You may change the tree in place.

An empty tree stays empty. Trees are shown in level order, like [5, 3, 8, 1, 4, null, 9], where null marks a missing child. Your function receives and returns real TreeNode objects with val, left and right.
constraints: The tree is at most 500 levels deep.

examples.explanation: 5 stays on top and its children swap: 8 left, 3 right. Below them the same happens: 9 moves to 8's left, and 3's children become 4 then 1. The bottom row 1, 4, 9 now reads 9, 4, 1.
A lone left child becomes a lone right child, so the swap must also work when the other child is missing.

hints: Hold the first example up to a mirror. The top box stays put. Where does box 1, bottom-left, end up?
Box 1 moves to the bottom-right. That needs 3 to move to the right side and 1 to move right under 3. So the swap happens at every node, not only the top.
Each subtree is a smaller design that also needs mirroring. If both subtrees were already mirrored, what would be left to do at the root?

For a null node return null. Otherwise mirror both subtrees, then attach the mirrored right as the new left child and the mirrored left as the new right child. Save one side in a variable before overwriting it.
bruteForce: You could read the tree into rows, reverse each row, and rebuild. But that means keeping every empty slot, and the slots double at every level, so a lopsided tree with 1,000 people can have rows far bigger than the tree. You never need the rows: swapping the two child pointers at every node, once, flips the whole picture in O(n) with no copies.

js: *   this.val = val; this.left = left; this.right = right;
* TreeNode is already defined for you.
py: # TreeNode is already defined for you.
def mirror_design(root: TreeNode | None) -> TreeNode | None:

js: const left = mirrorDesign(root.left);   // mirror each side first
py: left = mirror_design(root.left)    # mirror each side first
walkthrough: A mirrored tree is the root, with the mirrored right subtree on its left and the mirrored left subtree on its right.
1. Mirror the subtree at 3. Leaves 1 and 4 mirror to themselves, then swap: 3 has 4 on the left and 1 on the right.
• Mirror the subtree at 8. Its only child 9 moves from right to left.
• At 5, swap the finished subtrees: 8 goes left, 3 goes right.
The result, level by level, is [5, 8, 3, 9, null, 4, 1]. Writing root.left = mirror(root.right) without saving the original left first would lose that subtree before you mirrored it.
solution.timeWhy: Each node is visited once and does one swap.
solution.spaceWhy: The recursion stack, one call per level of the current path; h is the tree's height.
solution.takeaway: When a change to the whole tree is the same small change at every node, apply it at each node during one traversal. Swap, flip, relabel: visit every node once and act locally.
